\title{What a Class Description Buys:\\
       Alignment, Not Wording, in Zero-Shot Taxonomy Classification}

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{abstract}
Zero-shot classification against a taxonomy usually embeds a short
description of each class and ranks the descriptions against the document.
How much the wording of those descriptions matters is rarely measured. We rewrite the class descriptions of a NACE Rev.~2 taxonomy
over German trade register texts, from category labels into definitions that
enumerate concrete activities, and gain \ContentEffect~points of Top-1 accuracy.
A control shows the gain is not linguistic: rendering the same content in the
language of the documents is worth \LanguageEffect~points ($p =
\LanguageP$). We identify what does explain it---how far the rewrite moves each
class vector toward the centroid of the documents it must attract
($\rho = \AlignRho$ over \NCLASSES\ classes)---and show the
account is monotone across three corpora, one of which we predict before
measuring---and breaks on a fourth, registered in advance, where the alignment
change is negative and the gain is not. On \ArxivN\ arXiv abstracts with
author-assigned labels and arXiv's own category descriptions, both registered
predictions hold: a class text that moves the vectors \ArxivSpellAlign\ is
worth \ArxivSpellGain~points and one that moves them \ArxivDescAlign\ is worth
\ArxivDescGain, and the class-level relation replicates at $\rho = \ArxivRho$
over \ArxivRhoN\ categories. It cannot be optimised per class: three selection
criteria, including direct optimisation of development accuracy, fail to
generalise. Moving class vectors toward unlabelled documents confirms the
class-level relation in four preregistered studies on three encoders, while the
corpus-level ordering holds only once; and a character n-gram ranker over the
same descriptions matches the embedding system and gains as much from them.
\end{abstract}

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Introduction}

Assigning economic activity codes to free-text company descriptions is a
routine task for statistical offices, business registries and commercial data
providers, and a poorly supervised one: labelled examples are expensive,
taxonomies are revised, and the classes number in the tens or hundreds. The
standard remedy is zero-shot classification against the taxonomy itself. Each
class is represented by a short natural-language description, both description
and document are embedded by a sentence encoder, and the document is assigned to
the nearest class.

The class descriptions in such a pipeline are usually inherited rather than
designed: from the taxonomy's own published labels, an internal glossary, or
whoever set the system up. Their wording is treated as a configuration detail
rather than a modelling decision, and we are not aware of a study that measures
how much it costs to get wrong. This paper argues it is the largest single lever
in the pipeline, and identifies the quantity that governs it.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
  \item Rewriting class descriptions from category labels into definitions that
        enumerate concrete activities gains \ContentEffect~points of Top-1
        accuracy on NACE section assignment, validated on a held-out half of the
        evaluation set that was never inspected during the rewrite.
  \item A control separating content from language. Sixteen of twenty-one
        descriptions were in a language none of the documents were written in,
        which is an attractive explanation and the wrong one: the same content
        rendered in the documents' language is worth \LanguageEffect~points.
  \item A mechanism. The gain is predicted by how far the rewrite moves the
        class vector toward the centroid of its own documents
        ($\rho = \AlignRho$), the only candidate of five that holds within
        each corpus separately. Because it was found by search, we rest it on
        the preregistered test below rather than on its own $p$-value.
  \item Prospective tests on three further corpora, each registered before its
        accuracy was computed: a confirmation on Reuters, a failure of the
        corpus-level prediction on Brown, and on \ArxivN\ arXiv abstracts with
        author-assigned labels and arXiv's own class descriptions, a class text
        worth \ArxivSpellGain~points and one worth \ArxivDescGain, each as its
        alignment change implied.
  \item Four preregistered, label-free interventions on the class vectors,
        moving each toward its nearest unlabelled documents. The first raises
        accuracy in the order the alignment change predicts, including on the
        corpus where written definitions did not help. Across all four, on three
        encoders, the class-level prediction holds every time and the
        corpus-level ordering once, which we report as the account's limit.
  \item A negative result with a measured cause: the quantity cannot be
        optimised per class, because the classifier's argmax compares across
        classes on a scale that depends on description style.
  \item Stronger references and alternatives. A character n-gram ranker over
        the same descriptions matches the system and gains as much from the
        rewrite, a classifier trained on most of the labels does no better, and
        an instruction-tuned model asked for the section directly does not beat
        the system at Top-1.
  \item A test of who writes the descriptions: definitions written by a model
        from a different family than the labeller, from the control text alone,
        gain in the predicted direction but recover \SourceWriterShare\ of the
        gain.
\end{itemize}

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Classifying from the meaning of the class.}
Assigning documents to classes with no labelled examples, using only what the
class name means, was introduced as \emph{dataless} classification
\citep{chang-etal-2008-importance} and extended to hierarchies
\citep{song-roth-2014-dataless}; both represent class and document in a shared
semantic space and take the nearest class. Contemporary practice replaces that
space with a pretrained encoder \citep{devlin-etal-2019-bert}, most often a
sentence encoder trained with a contrastive sentence-level objective
\citep{reimers-gurevych-2019-sentence}, and multilingual settings use either a
jointly pretrained encoder \citep{conneau-etal-2020-unsupervised} or one
distilled into new languages \citep{reimers-gurevych-2020-making}. An
influential alternative recasts the decision as entailment between the document
and a hypothesis built from the class \citep{yin-etal-2019-benchmarking}. What
these share is that the class is represented by text someone wrote, and that the
text itself is treated as given: the reported comparisons vary the encoder, the
scoring function or the calibration, not the description.

\paragraph{The wording of the label, as prompt engineering.}
That the surface form of a label matters is well established for prompted
language models. Verbalizers are hand-designed \citep{schick-schutze-2021-exploiting},
searched automatically over single tokens \citep{schick-etal-2020-automatically},
or optimised as discrete triggers \citep{shin-etal-2020-autoprompt}; prompt and
demonstration selection can be tuned jointly with the model
\citep{gao-etal-2021-making}, and the resulting systems are famously sensitive
to incidental choices such as the order of examples
\citep{lu-etal-2022-fantastically}. This sensitivity is not the same thing as
sensitivity to \emph{meaning}: \citet{webson-pavlick-2022-prompt} show that
models can perform as well with irrelevant or actively misleading prompts as
with sensible ones, which makes the semantic content of a label an open question
rather than a settled one. Our setting isolates it: with no prompted model, no
in-context example and no token search---a description enters only as an
embedding---a change in the description can act only through what it means.

\paragraph{Keyword extraction.}
The keyword-extraction literature is adjacent and instructive. KeyBERT
\citep{grootendorst-2020-keybert} scores candidate phrases by embedding
similarity to the document and admits a set of seed keywords intended to steer
extraction toward a domain; PatternRank \citep{schopf-etal-2022-patternrank}
constrains candidates by part of speech, PromptRank
\citep{kong-etal-2023-promptrank} scores them with a prompted language model,
and MDERank \citep{zhang-etal-2022-mderank} ranks by the effect of masking a
candidate out of the document. Purely statistical methods such as YAKE
\citep{campos-etal-2020-yake} remain competitive on short documents.
Closest to our setting, \citet{meisenbacher-etal-2024-improved} extract
class-specific keywords from the same register under the same 21-section scheme
(WZ~2008, the German edition of NACE Rev.~2), guiding KeyBERT with seed keywords
that are expanded iteratively, and evaluate the keywords against gold lists. The
pipeline studied here follows that design, but uses it to assign the section
rather than to extract its vocabulary. The seed
mechanism is the closest analogue to what we study---a hand-written vocabulary
supplied to steer an embedding-based decision---and we find it redundant for
classification once the descriptions carry the same information, which says
nothing about the keyword quality \citet{meisenbacher-etal-2024-improved}
measure.

\paragraph{Method of reporting.}
The prospective tests in Sections~\ref{sec:corpora} and~\ref{sec:rocchio} follow
the preregistration practice argued for by
\citet{van-miltenburg-etal-2021-preregistering}, whose costs and limits are
discussed by \citet{sogaard-etal-2023-two}. We adopt a lightweight form: the
prediction and the quantity it rests on are stated before the outcome is
computed, and for the label-free studies committed to version control with a
fingerprint of the method that the evaluation checks before it runs.
Comparisons between systems use paired tests rather than differences of point
estimates, as urged by \citet{dror-etal-2018-hitchhikers}, and label quality is
reported as chance-corrected agreement following \citet{artstein-poesio-2008-survey}. Every comparison
reported as a finding is collected in Appendix~\ref{app:effects} with a bootstrap
interval \citep{efron-1979-bootstrap}, and all \EffectTests\ tests are corrected
together with the Holm procedure \citep{holm-1979-simple}, fixed before the
adjusted values were seen; where the text relies on a comparison that does not
survive, it says so.

\section{Method}

A taxonomy assigns each of $K$ classes a name and, optionally, a description.
We form a class vector by encoding the concatenation of name and description,
and, in the configuration the system shipped with, averaging it with the
encoding of a hand-written seed keyword list:
\[
  v_c = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(f(\text{name}_c \Vert \text{desc}_c) + f(\text{seeds}_c)\big),
\]
where $f$ is the sentence encoder: paraphrase-\allowbreak multilingual-\allowbreak MiniLM-\allowbreak L12-\allowbreak v2
\citep{reimers-gurevych-2020-making}, with 118M parameters. Its larger sibling,
paraphrase-\allowbreak multilingual-\allowbreak mpnet-\allowbreak base-\allowbreak v2 (278M), is tested as an ablation.
A document $d$ is assigned to
$\arg\max_c \cos(f(d), v_c)$. Throughout the experiments that isolate the effect
of descriptions we drop the seed term, so that the quantity under test is the
only thing varying.

Our central measurement is the \emph{alignment} of a class vector with the
documents it should attract:
\[
  a(c) = \cos\!\big(v_c,\ \bar{d}_c\big),\qquad
  \bar{d}_c = \frac{\sum_{d \in D_c} f(d)}{\lVert \sum_{d \in D_c} f(d)\rVert},
\]
with $D_c$ the documents whose gold label is $c$. Rewriting a description
changes $v_c$ and therefore $a(c)$; we write $\Delta a(c)$ for that change.

Systems are compared with exact McNemar tests on the same documents, and
accuracies carry percentile bootstrap intervals. Agreement is Cohen's
$\kappa$ and correlations are Spearman's $\rho$, computed with scikit-learn
\citep{pedregosa-etal-2011-scikit} and SciPy \citep{virtanen-etal-2020-scipy}.
Every result is regenerated by two commands: \texttt{make reproduce} for the
systems and ablations, which takes about \ReproduceMinutes~minutes on a laptop
(\ReproduceCPU, \ReproduceCores\ cores) and, rerun from a clean clone without
the unreleased corpus, reproduces the committed predictions exactly; and
\texttt{make study} for the description studies, of which only the label-free
ones need the corpus itself, as their unlabelled pool.

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Data}

\paragraph{NACE over trade register texts.}
\CorpusSize\ German company purpose statements from the Handelsregister, to be
assigned to one of the \NSections\ NACE Rev.~2 sections
\citep{eurostat-nace-2008}. The evaluation set is
\NEVAL\ documents sampled from that corpus, stratified by predicted section and
split between low-margin and representative cases; no gold label was used in the
selection. Labels were produced by a language model (Claude, Anthropic) applying
a written annotation guideline, and validated by the author, who does not read
German and judged each document from an OPUS-MT English translation
\citep{tiedemann-thottingal-2020-opus}: in a blind pilot the author agreed with
the labeller on \PilotAgree\ of \PilotN\ documents ($\kappa = \PilotKappa$); after the
disagreements were adjudicated into three explicit rules, agreement on a fresh
\VerifyN-document sample was \VerifyAgree\ ($\kappa = \VerifyKappa$), rising to
\VerifyHighAgree\ on the documents
the labeller had flagged as high-confidence. Verified answers were promoted over
the machine labels in the released set. We report this in full because it
bounds every number that follows.

An earlier version of this evaluation set consisted of \RetiredN\ hand-written
documents rather than corpus samples. It was measurably easier---median
\RetiredMedianChars\ characters against \CorpusMedianChars, with
\RetiredBoilerplate\ carrying the legal boilerplate that \CorpusBoilerplate\ of
real entries carry---and the pipeline scored \RetiredTopOne\ on it against
\OldTaxonomyTopOne\ on the corpus-sampled set. We mention this because it is
the reason the evaluation set was rebuilt, and because it is a failure mode that is easy to reproduce
accidentally.

\paragraph{Two further corpora.}
20 Newsgroups \citep{lang-1995-newsweeder} (20 topical classes, English usenet
posts) and Reuters-21578, Distribution 1.0 \citep{lewis-1987-reuters} (12
frequent categories, single-label documents only, English financial newswire).
The three differ in what their class labels look like: abstract economic
categories, readable topic names, and opaque codes such as \texttt{money-fx}
respectively.

\paragraph{Held-out protocol.}
The description rewrite was motivated by reading errors, which is a form of
fitting. It was therefore developed on a stratified development half of the
NACE evaluation set and reported on a held-out half that was not examined.

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Language or content?}

The rewritten descriptions changed two things at once: language, since sixteen
of twenty-one were originally in Turkish while every document is German, and
content, since terse category labels became definitions enumerating concrete
activities. Table~\ref{tab:descriptions} separates them. The control condition
renders the original labels literally in German---same wording, same terseness, no
machine-translation noise, and the five sections already in German carried over
untouched.

\input{tables/descriptions}

Language alone is worth \LanguageEffect~points ($p = \LanguageP$). Content is
worth \ContentEffect. A crossed design varying document language and description
language independently agrees: the richer descriptions win in both document
languages, so the diagonal a matching effect would produce does not appear. The
effect also survives a change of encoder, and of encoder family: content is
worth \MpnetContentEffect~points on the larger mpnet-base-v2
(\MpnetContentPStat) and \LabseContentEffect\ on LaBSE
(\LabseContentPStat), which is trained by translation ranking rather than by
distillation from the same teacher. Neither encoder shows the language effect
either.

\subsection{What predicts which classes gain}

Table~\ref{tab:predictors}, in Appendix~\ref{app:supporting}, relates the per-class gain to five candidate
predictors over \NCLASSES\ classes. The target is the share of \emph{available}
headroom a class captured rather than raw gain, since a class already near
ceiling cannot gain much and raw gain largely measures where a class started.

Only $\Delta a(c)$ correlates with the gain, and it is the only candidate that
holds within each corpus separately (Figure~\ref{fig:alignment},
Appendix~\ref{app:supporting}). Resampling the classes gives a
\CILevel\ interval of $[\AlignRhoLo, \AlignRhoHi]$ for $\rho$, a permutation test
gives $p = \AlignPermP$, and leaving out any one class keeps $\rho$ between
$\AlignLooMin$ and $\AlignLooMax$. It was, however, the best of five candidates,
and corrected together with every other test in the paper it is not significant
on its own (\HolmAlignStat); Section~\ref{sec:rocchio} therefore tests it
prospectively. Neither the lexical overlap between a class name and its
documents nor the confusability of the class vector predicts anything. Words
added correlates \emph{negatively}: the recipe is not to write more.

\subsection{Three corpora, one predicted in advance}
\label{sec:corpora}

If $\Delta a$ is the mechanism it should also account for differences
\emph{between} corpora, and it should predict rather than explain.
Table~\ref{tab:corpora}, in Appendix~\ref{app:brown}, reports all three. For Reuters, the alignment change was
computed and the prediction printed before accuracy was examined; the code that
enforces that ordering is released with the paper.

Elaboration is worth \ReutersGain~points on Reuters ($p < 0.001$) and
\NewsGain\ on 20 Newsgroups ($p = \NewsP$). The 20 Newsgroups definitions moved
their class vectors \emph{away} from their documents: twenty-three careful words
about baseball sit further from real usenet posts than the word ``Baseball''
does. Spelling a bare Reuters category code out into a readable name is worth a
further \ReutersCodeGain~points, the same identifier-to-name jump 20 Newsgroups
shows, and for the same reason.

\paragraph{A fourth corpus, and a failure.} Those three changes are well
separated, which keeps the test away from the case the account finds hardest: a
corpus whose change is small, where it must predict a small gain. Brown is that
case, its classes being genres. Its change is \BrownAlign, so the registered
prediction was no gain, and smaller than NACE's and Reuters' whatever happened.
\BrownHeld\ of \BrownPredictions\ held: accuracy rose \BrownDefGain~points
(\BrownDefPStat, \HolmBrownDefStat), a hair above Reuters, so both
corpus-level predictions failed, while the class-level one held a fourth time
($\rho = \BrownRho$, \BrownRhoPStat, \HolmBrownRhoStat). We do not claim the
corpus mean predicts a corpus's gain (Appendix~\ref{app:brown}).

\subsection{Gold labels, somebody else's descriptions, and a change of zero}
\label{sec:arxiv}

Three objections apply to everything above: \NEVAL\ documents, labels a model
produced, and descriptions written for the study by the assistant that wrote
them. One corpus answers all three and tests the case the account finds hardest.
We take \ArxivN\ arXiv abstracts in the \ArxivClasses\ Computer Science
categories (Table~\ref{tab:arxiv}, Appendix~\ref{app:brown}), labelled by the
primary category each paper's own authors chose at submission and kept only where the paper carries no second Computer Science
category, as in the Reuters study. The third class text is arXiv's published
description of the category, quoted verbatim---written for its submitters, and
uneven by nature: some enumerate a field, others give only an ACM subject
class.

Both predictions were registered from the alignment changes before accuracy was
computed, and \ArxivHeld\ of \ArxivPredictions\ held. Spelling \texttt{cs.CL}
out into \emph{Computation and Language} moves the class vectors
\ArxivSpellAlign\ and is worth \ArxivSpellGain~points (\ArxivSpellPStat); the
official description moves them \ArxivDescAlign---zero, for practical
purposes---and is worth \ArxivDescGain\ (\ArxivDescPStat,
\HolmArxivDescStat). This is the near-zero case the account had never been
tested on: it predicts almost nothing, and almost nothing happens. Across the
\ArxivRhoN\ categories with documents, the alignment change and the share of
headroom captured correlate at $\rho = \ArxivRho$ (\ArxivRhoPStat,
\HolmArxivRhoStat)---the class-level relation, found by search on NACE and not
significant there once corrected, replicated prospectively on labels we did not
make and text we did not write.

\subsection{Moving the vector without words}
\label{sec:rocchio}

Everything above rests on descriptions someone wrote. If alignment is the
mechanism, moving a class vector toward its documents should help by itself,
with no description and no label. We moved each terse class vector toward the
mean of its \RocchioK\ nearest documents in an unlabelled pool from the same
source, with the evaluation documents removed and both settings fixed in
advance. Before any accuracy was computed we measured the alignment change in
each corpus, derived \RocchioPredictions\ predictions from it, and committed them
(\RocchioRegistered) with a fingerprint of the method that the accuracy step
checks before it runs. Table~\ref{tab:rocchio}, in
Appendix~\ref{app:labelfree}, reports all four studies.

\RocchioHeld\ of the \RocchioPredictions\ predictions held
(Table~\ref{tab:rocchio}): accuracy rose on all three corpora, in the order the
alignment changes predicted, and across classes the alignment change
again predicts the share of headroom captured ($\rho = \RocchioRho$,
\RocchioRhoPStat). The 20 Newsgroups result is the one the account risked most
on: written definitions gained nothing there because they moved its vectors
away from its documents, and this update, which moves them toward them, gains.
On NACE the gain is small and not significant; a few nearest neighbours do not
recover the vocabulary its sections lack, and written definitions remain far
better there.

\paragraph{From the written definitions.} A second study applied the same
update, unchanged, to the written definitions, with its own predictions
committed (\RocchioDefRegistered) before its accuracy was computed.
\RocchioDefHeld\ of its \RocchioDefPredictions\ predictions held. The update
again raised accuracy on Reuters and on 20 Newsgroups, and across classes the alignment change again predicts
the share of headroom captured ($\rho = \RocchioDefRho$, \RocchioDefRhoPStat).
On NACE, however, accuracy changed by \RocchioDefNaceGain~points
(\RocchioDefNacePStat) although alignment rose, so the direction predicted
for NACE failed, and with it the predicted ordering. We did not anticipate
this. The class-level relation held in both studies; the corpus mean of the
alignment change, in the second, did not predict the corpus's gain. The account
orders classes within a corpus more reliably than it compares corpora.

\paragraph{On the larger encoder.} A third study repeated the first, unchanged,
on paraphrase-\allowbreak multilingual-\allowbreak mpnet-\allowbreak base-\allowbreak v2,
with its own predictions committed (\RocchioMpnetRegistered) before its accuracy
was computed. \RocchioMpnetHeld\ of its \RocchioMpnetPredictions\ predictions held: accuracy
rose on all three corpora, though the 20 Newsgroups gain does not survive
correction (\HolmMpnetNewsStat), and the per-class relation appeared a third
time ($\rho = \RocchioMpnetRho$, \RocchioMpnetRhoPStat), while the predicted
ordering failed again.

\paragraph{On another encoder family.} Both encoders above are distilled from
one teacher. A fourth study repeated the first on LaBSE, trained by translation
ranking, its predictions committed first (\RocchioLabseRegistered);
\RocchioLabseHeld\ of \RocchioLabsePredictions\ held. It gained
\RocchioLabseNewsGain~points on 20 Newsgroups (\RocchioLabseNewsPStat) and
\RocchioLabseNaceGain\ on NACE, but \emph{cost} \RocchioLabseReutersGain\ on
Reuters (\RocchioLabseReutersPStat, \HolmLabseReutersStat)---the first corpus
where moving the vectors toward their documents made the classifier worse---and
the class-level relation held a fourth time ($\rho = \RocchioLabseRho$,
\RocchioLabseRhoPStat). Across the four studies, on three encoders from two
training regimes, the class-level prediction held every time and the
corpus-level ordering once.
The two parameters were never tuned, which leaves open whether the behaviour is
the method's or that setting's: over a grid of $K \in \{\SweepKList\}$ and
$\beta \in \{\SweepBetaList\}$, the gain keeps the registered sign in
\SweepAgreeing\ of \SweepCells\ cells, and the registered setting is the
conservative one on NACE (grid \SweepNaceMin\ to \SweepNaceMax~points). No
cell is tested for significance and none enters the corrected family.

\subsection{It cannot be optimised per class}

If $\Delta a$ were locally causal, choosing each class's description by it should
beat a fixed policy. It does not. Three criteria of increasing strength---
marginal alignment, a contrastive margin against the other classes, and greedy
search directly on development accuracy---all fail to generalise. None beats
the fixed policy, and the contrastive one falls furthest behind it
($\ContrastiveNewsDelta$~points on 20 Newsgroups,
$p = \ContrastiveNewsP$, \HolmContrastiveStat).

Two causes, both measured. First, the styles do not share a similarity scale: in
a set where every other class carries an elaborated description, that half wins
\ElabShareNACE\ of argmax decisions on NACE and \ElabShareNews\ on 20 Newsgroups
against a fair share of \FairShare, the bias running in the direction alignment
predicts. Per-class standardisation does not rescue it, costing \ZScoreCost~points
on the best pure policy by discarding class priors. Second, there are $2^K$ configurations for $K$ classes;
development accuracy rises under greedy search and held-out accuracy does not
follow.

The practical consequence is that description style should be uniform across
classes. A set of individually better descriptions can classify worse than a set
of consistently written ones.

\subsection{The seed keyword lists are redundant}

With language-matched, informative descriptions in place, removing the
hand-written seed keyword lists entirely changes accuracy by
$\SeedRemoval$~points ($p = \SeedRemovalP$; Table~\ref{tab:ablation},
Appendix~\ref{app:supporting}); they help by \SeedDevHelp~points on
the development half and hurt by \SeedTestHurt\ on the held-out one, neither
significant, so the defensible claim is that they add nothing reliable rather
than that they harm. Seed-guided keyword extraction and a six-stage filter show
no effect in any configuration we tested, and translating each document into
English with OPUS-MT \citep{tiedemann-thottingal-2020-opus} first is the one
variant that raises accuracy, by \TranslateGain~points
($p = \TranslateP$)---a lead rather than a result.

\subsection{Against baselines}

\input{tables/baselines}

Table~\ref{tab:baselines} places the system against lexical and embedding
baselines. Top-3 accuracy of \OursTopThree\ is the operating point we would
argue for: the task admits genuine ambiguity, and a tool that proposes three
codes to a human coder is the realistic deployment. The lexical baseline there
matches whole words; Section~\ref{sec:references} gives it a fairer form.

\subsection{Stronger references}
\label{sec:references}

\input{tables/references}

Two questions are asked of any zero-shot result: was the lexical baseline given
a fair chance, and what would labels buy? Neither analysis was preregistered,
and both enter the corrected family. German builds words by compounding, so a
TF-IDF ranker that matches whole words never finds \emph{Boden} inside
\emph{Bodenbelagsarbeiten}. Over the same sector texts, German Snowball stems help
less than character 3--5-grams within word boundaries, which reach
\RefCharTopOne\ (\RefCharPStat\ against the system; Table~\ref{tab:references}):
a lexical ranker that sees inside compounds matches the embedding system. It
still needs the descriptions. The rewrite is worth \RefCharDescGain~points to it
(\RefCharDescPStat), against \RefEmbedDescGain\ to the embeddings. The lever is
the text of the class, not the model that reads it.

Labels buy little here. Trained out of fold on the evaluation labels
themselves, about \RefTrainLabels\ per fold, logistic regression on the same
embeddings reaches \RefLRTopOne\ (\RefLRPStat), and Naive Bayes on TF-IDF far
less (Table~\ref{tab:references}). With some sections represented by a handful of documents this is
a small-data reference, not a ceiling; but a supervised model given most of the
labels does no better than one written definition per class.

\subsection{Who writes the definitions}
\label{sec:source}

The definitions that carry the effect were drafted by the assistant that also
produced the labels, and it had seen the corpora: a bias it holds toward one
reading of a section would reach the labels and the definitions alike. To
separate them, \SourceWriter, the open model of Section~\ref{sec:llm} and not
of the labeller's family, was given the terse German control text alone -- no
corpus, no documents, no sight of the assistant's definitions -- and asked for a
NACE-style definition. Predictions were registered from the alignment changes
before any accuracy was computed, and \SourceHeld\ of \SourcePredictions\
held: both sets of definitions beat the control, in the predicted order, and
per class the alignment change again predicts the share of headroom captured
($\rho = \SourceRho$, \SourceRhoPStat). The direction does not depend on who
writes; the size does. The independent definitions gain
\SourceWriterGain~points (\SourceWriterPStat), about \SourceWriterShare\ of
the assistant's gain, in more than twice as many words per class
(Appendix~\ref{app:source}). Either the assistant writes better definitions or
it shares a bias with the labeller, and this experiment separates neither; what
it rules out is that the effect holds only for text from the labeller's own
family.

\subsection{An instruction-tuned model asked directly}
\label{sec:llm}

The obvious alternative to embedding class descriptions is to ask a language
model for the section. We gave \LLMModel, an open instruction-tuned model of
roughly 7B parameters from a different family than the labeller, the section
names and the document, and asked for the three most likely sections with
greedy decoding; the prompt is released with the code. It ran locally in about
\LLMMinutes~minutes, and \LLMOffFormat\ of its replies left the requested format.
It reaches \LLMTopOne\ Top-1 against \OursTopOne\ for the system, a difference
that is not significant ($p = \LLMP$), but only \LLMTopThree\ Top-3 against
\OursTopThree\ ($p = \LLMTopThreeP$; \HolmLLMTopThreeStat), and
\LLMVerifiedTopOne\ on the human-verified documents ($p = \LLMVerifiedP$). The two agree on the top section
for only \LLMAgreeShare\ of documents, so they fail on different ones. A second open model from a third
family, \LLMTwoModel\ (\LLMTwoParams), reaches \LLMTwoTopOne\ Top-1 and
\LLMTwoTopThree\ Top-3 (\LLMTwoPStat, \LLMTwoTopThreePStat), well below both.
Nor does the effect transfer by prompting: given the definitions the encoder
ranks instead of the section names, the 7B model falls to \LLMDefTopOne\
(\LLMDefPStat). That prompt is an order of magnitude longer and was not tuned,
so it bounds nothing about prompted models---only that the gain is not had by
pasting the descriptions into one.
It answers in format on every document, but only in float32: in half precision
on this machine it returns empty strings, so what a model can do and what a
harness lets it do are different measurements, and the precision is recorded
with the result. A classifier built from a 118M-parameter
encoder and one definition per class is therefore not outperformed at Top-1 by
either open model, one of them roughly sixty times its size, and it answers
about \BenchLLMTimes\ times faster per document (Section~\ref{sec:cost});
whether larger or proprietary models change that is not tested here.

\subsection{What a document costs}
\label{sec:cost}

Accuracy says which system is worth running; cost says whether it can be run.
Table~\ref{tab:cost}, in Appendix~\ref{app:cost}, measures both on the same machine and the same documents,
with the class vectors built once at start-up, as a service would build them.
One document costs \BenchCharMs~ms in the character n-gram space,
\BenchMiniLMMs~ms through the MiniLM encoder and \BenchLLMMs~ms through
\LLMModel. The language model is about \BenchLLMTimes\ times slower per
document than the encoder whose accuracy it does not beat, holds
\BenchLLMRam~MB of memory against \BenchMiniLMRam, and occupies
\BenchLLMDisk~MB on disk against \BenchMiniLMDisk. The lexical rankers need a
megabyte of committed statistics and no model at all.

The ordering matters for the argument rather than for the record: the claim of
this paper is about what a description buys, and the description is the cheapest
part of every system in the table. Latencies are medians over \BenchTimings\
timings of a warm process taking one document at a time; the batch column is
what a batch job gets instead.

\subsection{Checked against human-verified labels}
\label{sec:verified}

Only \VerifyN\ of the \NEVAL\ labels carry an answer a person checked, and they
were drawn half at random and half from the labeller's low-confidence cases, so
their absolute accuracy is not an estimate for the whole set. What they can
test is whether the conclusions depend on the model-produced labels. On those
documents alone the system scores \VerifiedTopOne\ (\CILevel\ interval
\VerifiedTopOneCI), against \RestTopOne\ on the rest. The central comparison
holds in direction: reverting to the previous, terse descriptions scores
\VerifiedOldTaxTopOne\ on the same documents ($p = \VerifiedOldTaxP$, exact
McNemar), though on so few documents it is not significant once corrected
together with everything else (\HolmVerifiedStat). Comparisons with smaller
effects, such as removing the description from the class vector
(\VerifiedNoDescTopOne, $p = \VerifiedNoDescP$), point the
same way but are not significant at this size.

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Error Analysis}

Fifty errors from the development half were coded one by one against a written
codebook, by the AI assistant named in the statement on AI use\ifdefined\ErrorCodingKappa,
and independently by the author, blind to that coding and working from English
translations; the two codings agree on \ErrorCodingAgree\ of \ErrorCodingN\ errors
($\kappa = \ErrorCodingKappa$)\else; the author did not code them independently\fi.

Seed leakage is the largest category at \SeedLeakShare\ (Table~\ref{tab:errors},
Appendix~\ref{app:supporting}), and the failures are lexical rather than
semantic: \emph{Bodenbelagsarbeiten} (floor covering, Construction) is drawn to
Mining because \emph{Boden} appears in that section's vocabulary. This converges
with the ablation from the other direction and is the second reason to drop the
seed lists. Ambiguous section definitions and genuinely multi-sector companies
account for a further \AmbigMultiShare, and no change to this system addresses
them: NACE admits two defensible answers for a company that both manufactures
and installs windows. We read that as a rough ceiling on single-label accuracy
here, and as the strongest argument for reporting Top-3.

% ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section{Conclusion}

What a class description buys a zero-shot classifier is alignment with the
documents it must attract, and its wording is a modelling decision rather than a
configuration detail. Where class names never appear in their documents, writing
that vocabulary down is worth \ContentEffect~points; where they are already the
documents' own words, the same work is worth nothing; and on arXiv, where the
official descriptions move the class vectors \ArxivDescAlign, they are worth
\ArxivDescGain. Which way a corpus goes is predictable from the alignment change
at the level of classes---in every corpus here, in every label-free study, and
most strongly where the labels and the descriptions are not ours
($\rho = \ArxivRho$)---but not from its corpus mean, which a fourth corpus
registered in advance contradicted. The quantity cannot be optimised per class
either, and neither an instruction-tuned model asked directly nor a classifier
trained on most of the labels beats one definition per class. The account orders
classes; it is weaker at comparing corpora, and we report it that way.

% ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
\section*{Limitations}

The evaluation labels are model-assisted rather than gold: produced by a
language model applying a written guideline, validated by the author on
\VerifyN\ documents at $\kappa = \VerifyKappa$, with \VerifyN\ of \NEVAL\ carrying human-verified
labels. The author does not read German and judged each document from a machine
translation, so translation errors enter the check itself. Any figure in this
paper should be read against that agreement, except those of
Section~\ref{sec:arxiv}, whose labels are author-assigned and whose class texts
are arXiv's. Section~\ref{sec:verified} repeats
the main comparisons on the human-verified documents alone; the central one
holds in direction, but at that size not once corrected for every other test.
Trained out of fold on these labels a supervised classifier reaches
\RefLRTopOne\ (Section~\ref{sec:references}), so they carry structure a model
can learn rather than noise; that is a weaker statement than a gold standard,
and it says nothing about the translation errors in the check.

The evaluation set is \NEVAL\ documents, and the width of every figure follows
from that: \OursTopOne\ Top-1 carries a \CILevel\ interval of \OursCI. Of the
\EffectTests\ comparisons reported as findings, \EffectNominal\ are
significant uncorrected and \EffectHolm\ after correction over the family, and
each that loses significance is qualified where it appears
(Appendix~\ref{app:effects}). A set of this size orders systems that differ by
tens of points; it cannot resolve differences of a few. It was not enlarged
after the fact: the predictions of every study registered against it were
committed before any accuracy on it existed, so replacing it would change what
those studies tested.

Agreement was measured between a human and the labeller, not between two humans.
The inter-annotator figure reviewers usually ask for would require a second
annotator who reads German; the released code prepares the blind sample for one.

The alignment account rests on five corpora. The alignment changes of the first
three are well separated ($\NaceAlignGain$, $\ReutersAlignGain$,
$\NewsAlignGain$), which is what makes the ordering visible and equally what
keeps the test away from the account's behaviour near zero. Brown was added for
that case and falsified the corpus-level prediction registered for it: a
negative alignment change with a positive gain (\BrownDefGain~points,
\BrownDefPStat), which does not survive correction (\HolmBrownDefStat) and so
is a nominal failure of a registered prediction rather than a strong refutation.
Either way we do not claim the corpus mean predicts a corpus's gain. The
near-zero case is no longer untested: on arXiv a change of \ArxivDescAlign\
came with a gain of \ArxivDescGain\ (Section~\ref{sec:arxiv}), which is the
account's least obvious prediction and the one corpus where it was checked
against labels nobody in this project produced. The class-level correlation holds within each corpus. On NACE, where it was
found by search, it does not survive correction on its own
(\HolmAlignStat); its prospective replications do, most clearly on arXiv
($\rho = \ArxivRho$, \HolmArxivRhoStat). Even there it orders classes rather
than determining them.

The class vectors, the documents and the alignment measure come from one
encoder at a time, and every preregistered study was run on a distilled
multilingual sentence-transformer. The description effect replicates on a
second encoder of that kind and on LaBSE, which is trained by translation
ranking instead, and it appears at a similar size in a character n-gram space
with no encoder at all (Section~\ref{sec:references}). The label-free test has
been run on three encoders and gives the same class-level result on each,
including on LaBSE, where it nonetheless cost \RocchioLabseReutersGain~points on
Reuters---the one corpus-and-encoder pair where moving the vectors toward their
documents hurt.

The cost figures in Section~\ref{sec:cost} come from one machine and one
implementation of each system; they order the systems, they do not fix absolute
values. Repeating the protocol on the same machine's GPU moves them---the
118M encoder goes from \BenchMiniLMMs\ to \BenchOtherMiniLMMs~ms per document,
the 278M one from \BenchMpnetMs\ to \BenchOtherMpnetMs---and leaves the
ordering of the \BenchOtherSystems\ systems \BenchOrderingHolds. A second
machine would be a better test than a second device on this one.

The instruction-tuned baselines are two open models, of roughly 7B and
\LLMTwoParams\ parameters, from families that are neither each other's nor the
labeller's. Larger or proprietary models may do better; the released code
includes an adapter for a paid API (\texttt{make llm-baseline}) that was not
run. Any such model has to come from a different family than the labeller, or it
is graded on its own answers. Both were run through one prompt and one decoding
setting, and the smaller one shows how much that harness can matter: in half
precision it answered nothing at all.

The label-free update in Section~\ref{sec:rocchio} is reported at one untuned
setting of its two parameters, chosen before any result; the grid around it
shows the sign of the gain is not an artifact of that choice, but a grid is a
robustness check and not a second preregistered test, and the one corpus where a
cell changes sign is 20 Newsgroups. On NACE it gains nothing significant from the terse labels
on either encoder, and loses accuracy from the written definitions, where its
prediction failed.
The update needs no labels; measuring alignment, and so testing the account, still does.

Finally, the per-class descriptions used in the elaborated conditions were
drafted by the AI assistant that also produced the labels, and it had seen the
corpora. Style is therefore controlled across conditions, but the descriptions
and the labels share a source: a bias that source has toward particular
readings of a section would reach both, and would flatter the descriptions it
wrote. Section~\ref{sec:source} bounds what that can explain rather than
removing it. Definitions written by a model from a different family, given the
control text alone, raise accuracy in the predicted direction, so the effect is
not confined to text from the labeller's family; but they recover only
\SourceWriterShare\ of the gain, and whether the rest is the assistant's
better writing or its shared bias is not separated by that experiment.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

The trade register corpus consists of public records describing companies rather
than individuals, though registered company names sometimes contain the names of
their owners. The collected sample is not redistributed, because its
redistribution licence has not been established; the vocabulary and inverse
document frequency statistics derived from it are released instead, which are
aggregate counts and cannot be inverted to recover the records. The exception
is the evaluation set: its \NEVAL\ records, \EvalShareOfCorpus\ of the sample, are
released with their labels so that every reported result can be checked. They
are entries in a public register, and company names are kept because they are
part of that record; the pipeline itself never reads them. The taxonomy, the
annotation guideline and all experiment code are released as well.

Top-1 accuracy is far below what unattended assignment of economic codes would
need. The system is meant to propose candidates to a human coder; used to
assign codes automatically, for example in official statistics, it would
propagate its errors silently. Both encoders are distributed under the Apache
licence. Reuters-21578 is distributed for research purposes only, by agreement
of Reuters Ltd. and Carnegie Group, and is used here for research alone.
20 Newsgroups is used as distributed through scikit-learn, whose distribution
states no licence.

\section*{Use of AI Assistants}

The author designed and directed this work: the author built the
keyword-extraction pipeline it starts from, with AI coding assistance; specified
its core evaluation, namely the baselines, the ablations and the error-analysis
categories; made the decisions on data release and disclosure; performed both
human verification passes described in the data section; and takes
responsibility for the content. In the study itself the author used Claude
(Anthropic), through Claude Code, for most of the experiment code and the
refactoring of the pipeline, the silver section labels under the annotation
guideline, the drafts of the rewritten and control class descriptions, the
coding of the errors in the error analysis, the analyses, and the draft of the
text.
No reported result was typed by hand: each is generated from the released
experiment outputs.
